Run Up to Elections 2019

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With 48 parties listed for the upcoming elections do you know who’s getting your vote or are you unsure? And how critical is your vote in determining an outcome?

Unique Selling Point:
The story will highlight the biggest demographic; women and the youth vote, paying attention to the youth and unemployment, who are according to political analyst Aubrey Matshiqi; ‘South Africa's ticking time bomb’. We will also look at a cross sections of the voters who represent some of our viewers.South Africans love voting and 70% of them go to the poles, so it is not so much about voter apathy according to political analysts, but rather about voter protest and how they will cast their vote in these upcoming elections

Summary:
Elections are looming and the big question; Who are you voting for remains unanswered by many. Some have opted to protest the elections and not vote due to an array of reasons all leading to hopelessness. But what happens to that vote that is wasted by not participating? Are you then responsible for perhaps an unexpected result that could shock us all? Our two political Analysts will unpack and inform us of these elements. Carte Blanche speaks to a representative cross section of the voters who unpack the issues that are concerning them.
It is election time and promises are the order of the day, but even in these promises that may or may not materialise it seems SA political parties are still missing what the key issues are and how to adequately tackle them. Their message to unemployed youth brings little hope to the hopeless graduates desperate for opportunities.
The 2019 elections are around the corner, but South Africa’s unemployed and disgruntled youth could be the ticking time tomb that shifts the status quo.

Further information:
1. YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT

Lesego Tau runs a youth NGO in Dobsonville, Soweto. What started as him helping young unemployed graduates apply for jobs and interact with government from a gogos four roomed house has now developed into an NGO where unemployed youth go to find assistance in job seeking. Lesego has hundreds of CVS of unempoloyed graduates loitering in Soweto, desperate to make use of their qualifications. He says political parties are not directly speaking to these youth who did everything they could to try and get qualified to be hired on merit but they face challenges. He says SA youth aren’t lazy or apathetic. Says the government offices are filled everyday with youth looking to drop off CVS. He speaks of the high cost of being unemployed. Having to travel to an internet café and spend money on looking for a job but yet these youth have little assistance. As a concerned resident he did what he expected government to do, bridge a gap through policy between youth particularly skilled youth and corporates. Lesego will provide one case study of an unemployed graduate who will speak to us about the struggle of being unemployed while qualified and their expectations from political parties if any. Political parties are offering jobs in their manifestos. We will find out from the case study if he believes this.
Visually it will be great to show how busy the streets of Dobsonville Soweto will be during the week, mid morning to reflect how many people are left home due to unemployment. The streets of Soweto will be bustling at what should be a quieter time with people ideally having gone to school and work. Lesego now works from a local community center in Dobsonville that has become a refuge for unemployed youth.


2. WOMEN
POWA- Rosie Motene (gender activist and director at POWA)
She talks about how political party manifestos don’t reflect what they implement on the ground and after elections. She gives examples of political apathy to gender based issues yet politicians need women to vote for them. However they are still not sending the right message to women. For instance that some of the big political parties don’t even have Sexual Harassment policies yet they campaign about ending gender based violence and inequality. She speaks women in politics who are protectors of patriarchy so when survivors of gender based violence see women in politics defending politicians who are found guilty of gender based violence (eg Mduduzi Manana). Allegations of sexual misconduct are not taken seriously because you have alleged perpetrators out there campaigning and speaking to women who are aware of the scandals. She speaks of the lack of political will to shift the gender issue which also spreads to the judiciary causing awful experiences for women who are victims of gender based violence. Motene says this years Gender Summit has proven to be another talk shop. So again politicians are missing the mark in terms of messaging which is what our political analyst Aubrey also said.

3. Aubrey Matshiqi – Political Analyst
Aubrey brings a sobering perspective to his analysis of the 2019 elections. He says that even though corruption is at the top of the list when it comes to electioneering, he believes the unemployed youth are a ticking time bomb and a portion of the electorate that has not been addressed or spoken to by the governing and oppositions parties and they pose a much greater threat to the stability of the country.
It is a misconception to thing that corruption is the biggest problem, inequality and unemployment are a far greater threat to our country. Unemployment is at a crisis level and will be a driver going forward. The youth are a catastrophe waiting to happen. The instability in poor communities will live beyond elections.
While women are the majority of voters they are invisible. The Women’s League still subscribes to patriarchal ideologies.
He also says that women are not being spoken to or their issues brought to light. In this he highlights that the governing party the ANC still does not have a sexual harassment policy in place.
This election is lacklustre. He sees no grand vision coming to the fore. The official opposition is unable to respond to the Cyril factor. He also believes this will be Musi Maimane’s last election as leader of the DA.
Aubrey says that on a national level the ANC are safe and that people have put faith in Ramaphosa, but on a provincial level thing are not as stable. The big areas of contentions will be Gauteng, Limpopo, North West and the Eastern Cape.
The smaller parties which are some of Zuma’s former supporters are part of a strategy to undermine the ANC and split the black vote.
Labour in general is in trouble, they are failing to attract young people.
He says the Socialist workers party is too late for these elections and that class is no longer a reliable predictor of what people are asking for.
South Africans love voting, so it is not voter apathy that will not lead people to the poles, but rather it will be a political choice. Very little left to believe in.
There is a generalised crisis in our politics, and the alternative parties are shallow and hollow unfortunately.


4. Busi Khaba (Political Analyst)
Busi had some fundamental opposing analysis as compared to Susan and Aubrey. Busi is predicting an election of coalition governments. She based this off the 2016 Local Government Elections, that saw the ANC having to humble itself and appeal to smaller parties to partner up into a coalition in order for the ANC to retain power in metros, but most importantly they lost key metros also due to coalitions. Busi believes, the local government elections were a starter for the provincial and national elections. She says because local gov elections are closer to the ground and reflect peoples patterns of voting. So she said it will be a “tight election” with no outright winner. Continuing with a government of coalitions.

Busi says CRs win within the ANC itself was a slim one (which it was). She says voters are smart and all the commissions and corruption scandals may finally catch up to the governing party. She says the Western Cape will be interesting to watch because the DA vote will be dented by Patricia de Lilles’ GOOD party, which may see more coalitions.
In terms of the youth vote Busi says this could significantly swing things because of the eligible voters the youth vote is the largest and could add a spanner to the works. She has statistics she says she will provide that show the number of eligible youth voters who she says are higher than before.
She says the ANCYL is pretty much none existent to the youth and doesn’t inspire hope in young people. How can a party with a dismal youth league promise to focus on youth issues when its own youth league doesn’t have a reputable leader? She says the opposition had an opportunity to shine bright these elections but have failed by their own doings, leaving voters with no credible viable option.
When it comes to women she says the political parties are merely ticking the boxes by speaking of women issues because in reality its not taken seriously. Giving an example of Bathabile Dlamini as Minister of Women having been a slap in the face to SA women after her SASSA scandal. She says there is nothing to show of what the department allocated to Women has done and many didn’t even know of its existence.

5. Abel Moloto: Is a 42 year old black male, who has an MBA, he spent 20 years in the USA getting educated and started a family there. Last year he decided to return to South Africa with his family as he was homesick and wanted to raise his family with his extended family here. He has sent out over 1000 applications since June last year looking for a job. He has been unable to find one, even though he is highly qualified. He is a conscientised voter and is disillusioned with the current government. He will be voting, but if he doesn’t find a job soon, he will have to return to the USA. We will film him driving along the highway where there are a lot of corporate offices where he tells us how many of his CVs are lying in each of those buildings.

6. We will speak to an older lady, coloured or Muslim, who can encapsulate their attitude to the upcoming elections. (still trying to get this case study,)

7. We will also speak to a 40 year old white male with a family who is disillusioned and can talk about the issues that are plaguing him.(still trying to get this case study)

8. We are speaking to a female graduate who is 29 years old, lives in Thembisa and was unable to find a job after her degree, so she started her own business making jam, but that too is failing in this economic climate, and she speaks about how difficult it is to run your own business. This addresses the issues that government has been trying to encourage SMMEs with little success as they are not given the tools or the knowledge to make their business work in the long run. She too is a voter and is unhappy with how the current government is running the country.

Press Release:


South Africa's democracy, a quarter of a century on... has the mood of our elections irreversibly shifted from voter euphoria to hopeless ritual? The run-up to this week's elections has been dominated by anger over corruption, mass unemployment and unrelenting inequality and with 48 parties contesting in this week's elections, voters are finding it harder to make a choice this time round, and struggling to believe that their votes really count.

Script:


START!!!!

LINK: Masa: The 2019 elections are looming,
amidst the backdrop// of corruption and commissions, a power utility that's threatening to collapse the country's economy and unemployment at an all time high.//

BEAT WITH VISUAL BREAK

//South Africans love to go to the poles and with an unprecedented 48 political parties, will we change the way we vote?

VO: Greg Smith lives in the north of Johannesburg and runs a family owned business. He wants government to strip away the red tape involved in skills development.

Masa: do you know who you'll be voting for?

Greg: at this moment i’m still feeling a bit of confusion but one thing’s for sure i will definitely be there on the day

Masa: Even though you're unsure.

Greg: if you look at the lengths that people went to to give people the freedom to choose, rather make some kind of choice than no choice at all.

VO: According to Political Analyst Professor Susan Booysen, a drop below 70% participation of the electorate in the upcoming elections, would be telling.

Susan: A spectacular percentage like 30% of voters in opinion polls are saying they might be voting but they don’t think any of their parties speak to their demands and they're not hopeful that any of them will do the job for them.

Greg: I do prefer some of the personalities in the smaller parties unfortunately especially with the bigger parties you have all these polarizing factors so that’s where i find myself quite adrift as to who exactly to vote for.

Masa: and does Cyril Ramaphosa appeal to you?

Greg: yes and no. It’s difficult for me to really buy into a billionaire president.

VO: Although some voters may be ambivalent, Independent Political Analyst Aubrey Matshiqi stresses, that we shouldn’t underestimate the Ramaphosa factor.

Aubrey: The reason it is regarded as the most competitive since 1994 and therefore a watershed election is the assumption that the ANC is going to suffer very deep losses; Until former president Jacob Zuma resigned in Feb 2018, I was certain that the ANC would be replaced by another party as the ruling party of SA. Since the election of Ramaphosa that is not the case.

LINK: Masa: Its around 11.30 in the morning in Dobsonville Soweto and there are people walking in the streets. You'd think its a public holiday or the weekend but it’s the middle of the week and many of these people are jobless.

VO: Lesego Tau runs a foundation in Dobsonville Soweto, that enables youth development and career building.

Lesego: Bachelors degree…. LLB all at home etc..

VO: He has hundreds of CVs of qualified youths who are frustrated because they are unemployed.

Lesego: When I ask them some say well I’ll see who I vote for and only if they impress me what does impress then mean? What are you looking for when they say impress? Most of them will speak about unemployment, poverty, lack of infrastructure so I’m asking why are political parties not responding to the needs.

VO: Ratiwe and Tyron are two of the many young people who approach Lesego to help them find work. At 29, Ratiwe Sehlata has two degrees, psychology and communication media studies.

Masa: Will you be voting this year

Ratiwe: I am not sure

Masa: Why

Ratiwe: I need someone to give me solutions here I got everything right I completed my schooling I don't have a child so here I am waiting for a job that probably not even going to come so I need results and that's the party that I am going to vote for.

Aubrey: Unemployment has become a key driver of poverty in SA and no party seems to have an answer for that which means the levels of youth underdevelopment and youth unemployment will deepen. This is why many voters tell you that he or she is confused.

VO: 21 year old Tyron Graham only managed to complete one year of study in civil construction and then ran out of funds, he’s been looking for a job for over a year.

Masa: Tyron are you going to be voting this year

Tyron: Nope I won't

Masa: Why

Tyron: Politicians always want us to help them but they are not doing anything in our communities to change the way we are living so I havent really had a reason to vote.

Masa: Would you say you have lost hope in South African politicians

Tyron: if something goes on for 20 years and I have only lived 20 years where is hope there?

Aubrey: I keep on insisting that youth underdevelopment in this country is a ticking time bomb, which means they will find alternative means of political engagement and this is where things like fees must fall was significant so they are not being apathetic when they don’t register or when they register but do not vote that’s a political act.

Tyron: They need my vote so I need to vote for them in order for them to get their positions but what about my position. I went to school I passed good grades but we are still not working we are still at home doing nothing.

VO: People throughout South Africa are struggling to find employment. 42 year old Abel Moloto sacrificed everything to study in America and is on the verge of attaining his doctorate. He has an MBA and worked in finance for global companies… After 20 years he’s come home to build a life for himself and his family.

Abel: I came back in June of last year Before coming back I started applying for work in SA there was nothing but I felt like once I arrive in SA I’'ll be able to connect with people more.

VO: After sending his CV out over 1000 times, Abel only received one response for an interview.

Abel: I’ve applied with every big company you can name in SA. All the big banks, they have 10 or 15 applications from me for different positions, there's a sacrifice in coming back because i was established in the US. I came back because i love SA and i wanted to contribute to SA and my wife was fully supportive of that.

Masa: So how do you feel when you hear our president saying we'd like to retain skills in south Africa, please do not leave for greener pastures

Abel: That’s a nice speech to say to people but eventually if you don’t show them where you are going with those promises, people are going to leave.

VO: Abel will stay to cast his vote on election day, but if he doesn’t find a job soon, he will have to return to America and join his wife and children. They couldn’t afford to stay in South Africa any longer.

Abel: My mum she's kind because she cries all the time because she doesn’t want me to go back to the US. My hope is that something will come up in the next few weeks, and i can call my wife to come back and my kids to come back.

VO: According to Aubrey, there is a false belief among voters that elections will deliver ‘change’, but it’s what happens between elections that impacts – ‘change’.

Aubrey: People are protesting against the under performance of the state but they are also protesting against the under performance of the economy, if we stay on the current trajectory SA is heading towards a perfect storm of discontent.

LINK: Masa: With women forming 52% of the electorate, are political parties sending them the right message and taking their concerns seriously or are they just paying lip service?

VO: Rosie Motene, from People Opposing Women Abuse, believes there is progress, but South African women are still being subjected to patriarchal structures, that don’t put women’s needs at the forefront.

Rosie: A lot of people think its a hashtag, that its a campaign. Our country is in a crisis and [03:35:32.16] when you look at the different political parties and gender based violence isn’t in the top 3. For us it should be number 1. Women are being raped and murdered on a daily basis and our country needs to stand up, our new president needs to take force on that.

Masa: As a woman voter, what message do you want to hear from political parties?

Rosie: I don’t want a message, I want to see action. I want to feel that when i walk down the street I’m not threatened because a brother is standing next to me. I want to know god forbid something happen to me and i walk into a police station I will be protected. I want our government to see us and respect us and acknowledge what we have to put on the table.

LINK: Masa: South Africa rates amongst the highest in the world when it comes to inequality, the gap between the haves and have nots is widening but the one place where we are equal is at the voting booth.

VO: Badrunnisa Scholtz lives in New-Claire Johannnesburg. When she voted in 1994 she hoped that her and her family’s life would improve.

Badrunnisa: Whenever they wanted the votes all the parties come too light and promise things and they don’t fulfill their promises. You can see how our places look, the water is running, the drains are blocked. You can’t even wash because the water comes out and it smells. The rats, the mice, they crawl up and go into your windows.

Masa: What are some of the other challenges you face as a pensioner?

Badrunnisa: The hospitals are smelly, the prisons are more clean than the hospitals. I've been working all my life and i'm still working and it’s not fair what they're doing to our pensioners. In the beginning they said free education there's no free education, then they said free medicine, there’s no free medicine. If you go through the hospital and you owe them for 3 months they won’t help you

Masa: are you going to be voting on the 8th of May?

Badrunnisa: yes i will be voting on the 8th of May, but not for the ANC, not for the DA.

VO: Many South Africans blame corruption and state capture, for the failure of government to deliver its mandate to the people.

Aubrey: One of the things the narrative of state capture has done is to give the false impression and false consensus that corruption is the main challenge facing SA and it is not. The main challenge facing SA is inequality and if we do not deal with inequality SA will burn.

VO: But who will make up the next parliament to face these challenges? There seems to be consensus amongst analysts, on the outcome of the 2019 general election.

Susan: I expect the ANC probably to get between 55 and 58% of the national vote. The DA around 20% , EFF probably almost doubling their 6% of the vote in previous elections and around 10% that could be split up between small parties. I would say its the ANC with an outright majority but an ANC that is weaKer than it was in elections 5 years ago.

Masa: Should the ANC win the elections can we expect Cyril Ramaphosa to still be the president?
Aubrey: Ramaphosa's greatest challenge at the moment is inside the ANC. He presides over a party that is split right in the middle. It is not a given that if the ANC wins this election Ramaphosa is the next president of the country. If he does win it is not a certainty that he will finish his term.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 07 June 2019 Press Release: South Africa's democracy, a quarter of a century on... has the mood of our elections irreversibly shifted from voter euphoria to hopeless ritual? The run-up to this week's elections has been dominated by anger over corruption, mass unemployment and unrelenting inequality and with 48 parties contesting in this week's elections, voters are finding it harder to make a choice this time round, and struggling to believe that their votes really count. Script: START!!!! LINK: Masa: The 2019 elections are looming, amidst the backdrop// of corruption and commissions, a power utility that's threatening to collapse the country's economy and unemployment at an all time high.// BEAT WITH VISUAL BREAK //South Africans love to go to the poles and with an unprecedented 48 political parties, will we change the way we vote? VO: Greg Smith lives in the north of Johannesburg and runs a family owned business. He wants government to strip away the red tape involved in skills development. Masa: do you know who you'll be voting for? Greg: at this moment i’m still feeling a bit of confusion but one thing’s for sure i will definitely be there on the day Masa: Even though you're unsure. Greg: if you look at the lengths that people went to to give people the freedom to choose, rather make some kind of choice than no choice at all. VO: According to Political Analyst Professor Susan Booysen, a drop below 70% participation of the electorate in the upcoming elections, would be telling. Susan: A spectacular percentage like 30% of voters in opinion polls are saying they might be voting but they don’t think any of their parties speak to their demands and they're not hopeful that any of them will do the job for them. Greg: I do prefer some of the personalities in the smaller parties unfortunately especially with the bigger parties you have all these polarizing factors so that’s where i find myself quite adrift as to who exactly to vote for. Masa: and does Cyril Ramaphosa appeal to you? Greg: yes and no. It’s difficult for me to really buy into a billionaire president. VO: Although some voters may be ambivalent, Independent Political Analyst Aubrey Matshiqi stresses, that we shouldn’t underestimate the Ramaphosa factor. Aubrey: The reason it is regarded as the most competitive since 1994 and therefore a watershed election is the assumption that the ANC is going to suffer very deep losses; Until former president Jacob Zuma resigned in Feb 2018, I was certain that the ANC would be replaced by another party as the ruling party of SA. Since the election of Ramaphosa that is not the case. LINK: Masa: Its around 11.30 in the morning in Dobsonville Soweto and there are people walking in the streets. You'd think its a public holiday or the weekend but it’s the middle of the week and many of these people are jobless. VO: Lesego Tau runs a foundation in Dobsonville Soweto, that enables youth development and career building. Lesego: Bachelors degree…. LLB all at home etc.. VO: He has hundreds of CVs of qualified youths who are frustrated because they are unemployed. Lesego: When I ask them some say well I’ll see who I vote for and only if they impress me what does impress then mean? What are you looking for when they say impress? Most of them will speak about unemployment, poverty, lack of infrastructure so I’m asking why are political parties not responding to the needs. VO: Ratiwe and Tyron are two of the many young people who approach Lesego to help them find work. At 29, Ratiwe Sehlata has two degrees, psychology and communication media studies. Masa: Will you be voting this year Ratiwe: I am not sure Masa: Why Ratiwe: I need someone to give me solutions here I got everything right I completed my schooling I don't have a child so here I am waiting for a job that probably not even going to come so I need results and that's the party that I am going to vote for. Aubrey: Unemployment has become a key driver of poverty in SA and no party seems to have an answer for that which means the levels of youth underdevelopment and youth unemployment will deepen. This is why many voters tell you that he or she is confused. VO: 21 year old Tyron Graham only managed to complete one year of study in civil construction and then ran out of funds, he’s been looking for a job for over a year. Masa: Tyron are you going to be voting this year Tyron: Nope I won't Masa: Why Tyron: Politicians always want us to help them but they are not doing anything in our communities to change the way we are living so I havent really had a reason to vote. Masa: Would you say you have lost hope in South African politicians Tyron: if something goes on for 20 years and I have only lived 20 years where is hope there? Aubrey: I keep on insisting that youth underdevelopment in this country is a ticking time bomb, which means they will find alternative means of political engagement and this is where things like fees must fall was significant so they are not being apathetic when they don’t register or when they register but do not vote that’s a political act. Tyron: They need my vote so I need to vote for them in order for them to get their positions but what about my position. I went to school I passed good grades but we are still not working we are still at home doing nothing. VO: People throughout South Africa are struggling to find employment. 42 year old Abel Moloto sacrificed everything to study in America and is on the verge of attaining his doctorate. He has an MBA and worked in finance for global companies… After 20 years he’s come home to build a life for himself and his family. Abel: I came back in June of last year Before coming back I started applying for work in SA there was nothing but I felt like once I arrive in SA I’'ll be able to connect with people more. VO: After sending his CV out over 1000 times, Abel only received one response for an interview. Abel: I’ve applied with every big company you can name in SA. All the big banks, they have 10 or 15 applications from me for different positions, there's a sacrifice in coming back because i was established in the US. I came back because i love SA and i wanted to contribute to SA and my wife was fully supportive of that. Masa: So how do you feel when you hear our president saying we'd like to retain skills in south Africa, please do not leave for greener pastures Abel: That’s a nice speech to say to people but eventually if you don’t show them where you are going with those promises, people are going to leave. VO: Abel will stay to cast his vote on election day, but if he doesn’t find a job soon, he will have to return to America and join his wife and children. They couldn’t afford to stay in South Africa any longer. Abel: My mum she's kind because she cries all the time because she doesn’t want me to go back to the US. My hope is that something will come up in the next few weeks, and i can call my wife to come back and my kids to come back. VO: According to Aubrey, there is a false belief among voters that elections will deliver ‘change’, but it’s what happens between elections that impacts – ‘change’. Aubrey: People are protesting against the under performance of the state but they are also protesting against the under performance of the economy, if we stay on the current trajectory SA is heading towards a perfect storm of discontent. LINK: Masa: With women forming 52% of the electorate, are political parties sending them the right message and taking their concerns seriously or are they just paying lip service? VO: Rosie Motene, from People Opposing Women Abuse, believes there is progress, but South African women are still being subjected to patriarchal structures, that don’t put women’s needs at the forefront. Rosie: A lot of people think its a hashtag, that its a campaign. Our country is in a crisis and [03:35:32.16] when you look at the different political parties and gender based violence isn’t in the top 3. For us it should be number 1. Women are being raped and murdered on a daily basis and our country needs to stand up, our new president needs to take force on that. Masa: As a woman voter, what message do you want to hear from political parties? Rosie: I don’t want a message, I want to see action. I want to feel that when i walk down the street I’m not threatened because a brother is standing next to me. I want to know god forbid something happen to me and i walk into a police station I will be protected. I want our government to see us and respect us and acknowledge what we have to put on the table. LINK: Masa: South Africa rates amongst the highest in the world when it comes to inequality, the gap between the haves and have nots is widening but the one place where we are equal is at the voting booth. VO: Badrunnisa Scholtz lives in New-Claire Johannnesburg. When she voted in 1994 she hoped that her and her family’s life would improve. Badrunnisa: Whenever they wanted the votes all the parties come too light and promise things and they don’t fulfill their promises. You can see how our places look, the water is running, the drains are blocked. You can’t even wash because the water comes out and it smells. The rats, the mice, they crawl up and go into your windows. Masa: What are some of the other challenges you face as a pensioner? Badrunnisa: The hospitals are smelly, the prisons are more clean than the hospitals. I've been working all my life and i'm still working and it’s not fair what they're doing to our pensioners. In the beginning they said free education there's no free education, then they said free medicine, there’s no free medicine. If you go through the hospital and you owe them for 3 months they won’t help you Masa: are you going to be voting on the 8th of May? Badrunnisa: yes i will be voting on the 8th of May, but not for the ANC, not for the DA. VO: Many South Africans blame corruption and state capture, for the failure of government to deliver its mandate to the people. Aubrey: One of the things the narrative of state capture has done is to give the false impression and false consensus that corruption is the main challenge facing SA and it is not. The main challenge facing SA is inequality and if we do not deal with inequality SA will burn. VO: But who will make up the next parliament to face these challenges? There seems to be consensus amongst analysts, on the outcome of the 2019 general election. Susan: I expect the ANC probably to get between 55 and 58% of the national vote. The DA around 20% , EFF probably almost doubling their 6% of the vote in previous elections and around 10% that could be split up between small parties. I would say its the ANC with an outright majority but an ANC that is weaKer than it was in elections 5 years ago. Masa: Should the ANC win the elections can we expect Cyril Ramaphosa to still be the president? Aubrey: Ramaphosa's greatest challenge at the moment is inside the ANC. He presides over a party that is split right in the middle. It is not a given that if the ANC wins this election Ramaphosa is the next president of the country. If he does win it is not a certainty that he will finish his term. FIN!!!!!!!

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The story will highlight the biggest demographic; women and the youth vote, paying attention to the youth and unemployment, who are according to political analyst Aubrey Matshiqi; ‘South Africa's ticking time bomb’. metadata.Summary: Elections are looming and the big question; Who are you voting for remains unanswered by many. Some have opted to protest the elections and not vote due to an array of reasons all leading to hopelessness. But what happens to that vote that is wasted by not participating? Are you then responsible for perhaps an unexpected result that could shock us all? Our two political Analysts will unpack and inform us of these elements. Carte Blanche speaks to a representative cross section of the voters who unpack the issues that are concerning them. It is election time and promises are the order of the day, but even in these promises that may or may not materialise it seems SA political parties are still missing what the key issues are and how to adequately tackle them. Their message to unemployed youth brings little hope to the hopeless graduates desperate for opportunities. The 2019 elections are around the corner, but South Africa’s unemployed and disgruntled youth could be the ticking time tomb that shifts the status quo.
